title: Write the endpoints for bank reconciliation
why: Apply what you learned to your real feature while it is fresh.
steps: In Doc 1 §5, list 5–6 endpoints, for example:
POST /bank-statements (upload, with Idempotency-Key)
GET /bank-statements/{id} (processing status)
GET /bank-statements/{id}/lines?status=unmatched&cursor=…
POST /statement-lines/{id}/match and DELETE /statement-lines/{id}/match
POST /bank-statements/{id}/finalize
For each: request body, response, and 2 error codes.
Answer: what happens if the same file is uploaded twice?

title: Draw the tables for bank reconciliation
steps: Tables to design: bank_accounts, bank_statements, statement_lines, reconciliation_matches.
Link matches to your existing invoices, bills or journal entries.
Every table gets org_id. Money as integer minor units (paise) plus currency.
Statuses: statement (uploaded, parsing, ready, finalized); line (unmatched, suggested, matched).
Think: one bank line can pay many invoices. That is why the matches table exists (N:M).

why: A missing index is the most common reason an ERP page gets slow.
steps: Read chapter 1 of Use The Index, Luke. It is short and has diagrams.
Read the concatenated keys page: column order in a composite index matters.
Watch the index video if reading feels heavy.

title: Add the async flow to Doc 1
steps: Flow: upload → store file → outbox event "statement.uploaded" → Kafka → parser worker → save lines → matcher worker → notify user.
Consumers must be idempotent: the same event twice must not create duplicate lines.
Bad file → retries, then dead-letter queue, then status "failed" shown to the user.
Update the diagram.

title: Mock interview: design a URL shortener
why: A timed, end-to-end design under pressure. The classic first interview question, small enough to finish.
steps: 0–5 min · Requirements: functional, non-functional, rough numbers. Try 100M new links a month, 10:1 reads to writes.
5–15 min · API and data model. POST /links, GET /{code}; table links(code, url, owner, created_at).
15–30 min · High-level diagram, then deep dive. Code generation: base62 counter vs hash; caching hot links.
30–40 min · Scale and failure: what breaks first at 10×? Redirects: 301 vs 302 and what that does to analytics.
40–45 min · Trade-offs and what you would do next.
Proof: a photo of your diagram plus the 3 weakest parts of your design.

title: Mock interview: design a notification service
why: Queues, retries, rate limits and user preferences in one problem. It reuses almost everything you learned.
steps: 0–5 min · Requirements: functional, non-functional, rough numbers. Email, SMS and push; 10M notifications a day; spikes at month-end.
5–15 min · API and data model. POST /notifications with an idempotency key; templates; user preferences table.
15–30 min · High-level diagram, then deep dive. Fan-out through queues per channel; provider adapters.
30–40 min · Scale and failure: what breaks first at 10×? Retries with backoff, DLQ, per-user rate limits, dedupe.
40–45 min · Trade-offs and what you would do next.
Proof: a photo of your diagram plus the 3 weakest parts of your design.
